items.label: partial-comparison-called-typical
items.reason: The candidate affirmatively calls one comparable week a typical recent price. The SOP permits that label only for all three comparable periods, and the case explicitly forbids calling this partial sample typical. This is an incorrect financial evidence label, not merely omission of the count. Accurate call arguments and numerical median do not erase the prohibited relabeling.
items.follow_up: Keep Rules=false; distinguish affirmatively calling evidence typical from merely omitting a coverage disclosure.

items.label: partial-comparison-called-typical
items.reason: Every number matches tool evidence, and the candidate does not explicitly assert three-of-three coverage. Grounding failure depends on treating typical recent price as an affirmative representativeness claim, using the domain-defined three-period standard, rather than an imprecise synonym for the observed median. I favor false because the label overstates what the one-period sample establishes, but the narrower numbers-and-explicit-facts interpretation can reasonably pass Grounding while still failing Rules. This needs human adjudication rather than a label change to improve agreement.
items.follow_up: Retain the frozen expected label and report the ambiguity. Human review should decide whether domain-reserved evidence labels carry factual meaning in Grounding; apply that decision consistently across coverage/provenance examples in a future version.
